title: Understanding Physical and Psychological Distances to Food
text: Farms are an interesting part of this. There was a time when people were very close to their food. They were physically close to it and psychologically close to it. The food was raised locally. Excuse me. If you think back to New Haven in the 1950s or 1940s, or 1930s, a lot of the food, much more then is the case today, was grown locally and was sold in markets and so there might have been one person or one step that resided between you and your food. You might even see the farmers sometimes who brought the food into market, and that was certainly true in earlier days. The distance to food has changed a lot because food has to come in from far greater distances than used to be the case, and that's changed our relationship with food a lot, into a distant rather than a close relationship. Here's an example that highlighted in the block there are the — is a farm called Fairview Gardens, that's outside of Los Angeles, in suburban Los Angeles, and so that's — the bracketed part is the farm in 1954. The next slide shows the farm, same farm and its surroundings in 1998, so you can see that a lot has happened here. This means that all the area surrounding that Fairview Gardens was mainly farmland back in the 1950s, all growing food, probably a fair amount of it being eaten locally by people. points: People used to be physically and psychologically close to their food, and that distance has grown, changing our relationship with food.
In New Haven in the 1930s to 1950s much more food was grown locally and sold in markets, often with only one step between you and your food.
You might even see the farmers who brought the food to market.
Now food travels far greater distances, so the relationship has become distant rather than close.
Example: Fairview Gardens, a farm near Los Angeles, was surrounded by farmland in 1954, but by 1998 development had replaced it, so food must come from further away.
